chapter: Glen Island, early records and Duke Ellington
title: Who publishes discographies: Bob Haring, Feather and Brunswick labels
summary: He describes a Florida discographer who also bootlegs, a set omitting jazz bands, Bob Haring as most-recorded leader, and how Brunswick used multiple labels.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Yeah. Where are they published and by whom, the discographies?

Well, one guy is in Florida. He's also putting out bootleg records at this time. And this other is a regular, handsomely bound, there's two books, they're quite thick, and I got them -- I noticed them advertised in one of the book things that we get in the mail, and it has every band that ever recorded anything, except that it does not cover jazz. They do not cover Duke in there, they do not cover Basie. In other words, what they call

out and out jazz bands. They -- it also says in there that these have been covered very thoroughly elsewhere. But there's all sorts of bands there. Did you know that the guy that made the most records of anybody, do you know what his name is? The orchestra? Bob Haring, H-a-r-i-n-g.
There's something like 40 pages of things that were recorded under his name. I knew of him, vaguely. I never met him. But I was looking through this the other day and I couldn't believe this.
However, those, there again, you'll see big gaps in there. Unknown, unknown, you know. And it's --
Who is the guy in Florida who has done one? His is the one that goes to '42?
No, he goes right up to today. Up till through '67. I can't tell you his name offhand, but besides, I just said he's putting out bootleg records, and I don't --
This material is kept confidential. As confidential as you want it to be. It's up to you what happens to this material.
I really don't remember his name. I could supply it to you, but I don't have it --
It would be interesting to know. And
also know that the personnel was not --

Well, Leonard Feather had one out, called, "The Hot Discography," or something like that, and I don't believe it went any further than maybe in the mid-'40s or something like that. I think it was his first thing he put out. Now, he may have updated it.
Not to my knowledge. I don't think so. Was it more accurate than these others?

It was pretty accurate, yeah. However, when you get back in the murky areas, you get back too far, he suffers from the same thing, probably lack of records on the part of the recording companies, plus the fact that people have passed on and there isn't anybody to ask. The same thing you're having the problem with me, I can't remember the name of this guy when I know him very well, you know, or that guy.
Well, at least we have the names of the labels that you recorded for during that period. So --

When you recorded for Brunswick there you had no idea what label you were on, because you might be on Perfect Records in one town, Mellotone in another, and Vocalion in another, and Auriole in another. They had all of these multiple labels, so that there was no way of telling. And it was all the same date. So if you called a record company, to me, it really wouldn't mean much, unless it was one of the big three of the time, you know, like Victor, Columbia and Decca, or something like that.
